title: WHO: South-East Asia had 47% of world measles cases in 2025
excerpt: WHO's global measles report says South-East Asia had 4.6 million cases in 2025 despite 96% coverage, as Bangladesh's measles deaths reach 1,378.

image.alt: A freezer truck for delivering vaccines to health facilities in Bangladesh
image.credit: File photo: USAID / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

content:
DHAKA, 28 November 2026: The WHO South-East Asia Region, which includes Bangladesh, had an estimated 4.6 million measles cases in 2025, 47% of the world total, even though it has the highest vaccination coverage of any region, the World Health Organization (WHO) said in its annual global measles report on Friday (27 November). The report warns that high regional averages "can mask disparities among countries and at the subnational level", which it says contributed to "multiple outbreaks and continued endemic measles transmission" in the region in 2026.

Worldwide, WHO estimates that 72,000 people died of measles in 2025, a 91% fall since 2000, and that vaccination has saved more than 60 million lives since 2000. About 10 million people were infected. Global coverage was unchanged: 84% of children received a first dose and 77% a second, and more than 29 million children were unvaccinated or under-immunised. "Measles does not forgive complacency," said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General.

In the South-East Asia Region, first-dose coverage was 96% and second-dose coverage 93% in 2025, according to the full report in WHO's Weekly Epidemiological Record. The region had an estimated 16,800 measles deaths, 23% of the global total. Only four of its countries, Bhutan, the Maldives, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea and Timor-Leste, are verified as having eliminated measles. "In countries with large birth cohorts, even relatively small pockets of under-vaccinated populations may represent hundreds of thousands of susceptible individuals capable of sustaining circulation of the virus," the report says.

The report does not name Bangladesh, and its outbreak counts cover only 2025. It says no country in the region reported a large or disruptive outbreak in 2025. Bangladesh's outbreak began in March 2026. In the 24 hours to 8am on Friday, seven more children died, taking suspected and confirmed measles deaths since 15 March to 1,378 (1,272 suspected, 106 laboratory-confirmed), The Business Standard reported, citing the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). Suspected cases reached 262,808 and confirmed cases 26,554.

Why it matters

WHO's analysis points to the question Bangladesh's health officials and experts are now asking: how an outbreak this large happened in a country that reported high national coverage. An IEDCR-led study reported this week found 24% of sampled children lacked protective antibodies, and cases kept rising despite the catch-up campaign. WHO's advice is to look below national averages, at upazila, ward and community level, and run targeted catch-up where gaps are found. For NGOs working in slums, char and haor areas and the Rohingya camps, that means helping find unvaccinated children.

What to watch

  • Whether the DGHS or WHO Bangladesh publish subnational coverage data or a review of why the campaigns fell short.
  • WHO/UNICEF national immunisation coverage estimates for 2026, usually published in July, which will show whether Bangladesh's reported coverage holds up.
  • The daily DGHS measles bulletin as the outbreak enters its ninth month.
